results.summary: This chip implements a spiking neural network reservoir computing core that detects atrial fibrillation and asystole from R-peak timing pulses. It uses eight LIF neurons with recurrent feedback and a readout stage that accumulates weighted spikes over fast and slow windows, requiring both windows to agree before raising an alarm. The design is configured by serially loading 33 bits of weights and is tested by applying synthetic R-peak pulses and observing the output flags and confidence score. Notable features include self-adapting neuron thresholds and a compact implementation in 959 logic cells, with no processor or software required.

This design is a streaming Sobel edge detection accelerator for grayscale images, using line buffers and a 3x3 sliding window to compute horizontal and vertical gradients in real time. Pixels are streamed in one per clock cycle, and the edge strength is output as an 8-bit value. The design is verified using cocotb with a Python golden reference model across several test patterns. No external hardware is required for simulation, and physical testing can use a standard Tiny Tapeout demo PCB.

This project implements an 8-bit square root calculator using the non-restoring algorithm, producing a Q4.4 fixed-point result. The user applies an 8-bit input via switches and pulses the start pin, then reads the 8-bit output on LEDs. The design operates at a 50 Hz clock and requires no special external hardware beyond the LEDs on the demo board. It is a straightforward arithmetic core with a simple start/done handshake.

This design is a 3x3 systolic array with 4-bit inputs that performs matrix multiplication, using output-stationary dataflow. It includes SPI communication to load matrices A and B and to read out the resulting 3x3 matrix. The design is tested via a provided Makefile test, and manual testing requires driving SPI signals with a clock at most half the system clock. No external hardware is required beyond the SPI host.

This project is a tetrahedral-style oscillator built from coupled CMOS inverter pairs with MIM capacitors as load elements, implemented in the SKY130 process. It provides four buffered observation outputs that oscillate around 12 MHz when powered from a 1.8 V supply. The design is tested by probing the outputs with a high-impedance oscilloscope or frequency counter, and no external passives or bias sources are needed. Post-layout extracted simulation was performed to verify oscillation.

This is a simple hello-world design that counts from 0 to 9 once per second on a single 7-segment display. It uses a clock divider to generate a 1 Hz tick, a digit counter, and a combinational 7-segment decoder. The design is intended to run on the Tiny Tapeout demo board, using the onboard 7-segment display and reset button, and can also be simulated with a cocotb testbench. It is notable as the creators' first silicon design project, prototyped on Wokwi.

This project is a VGA display that shows a checkers pattern, using the Tiny VGA pinout with 2-bit color per channel and sync signals. The documentation is essentially placeholder text (lorem ipsum), so the exact functionality and testing procedure cannot be determined from the provided information. The design likely generates a static or moving checkerboard pattern on a VGA monitor. No external hardware details are given beyond the VGA connection implied by the pin names.

This design is a 40-bit shift register with a hardcoded secret number, forming a challenge where the output goes high only when the correct 40-bit sequence is shifted in. The user shifts bits in serially, one per clock cycle, and after 40 bits the output indicates whether the sequence matches. The register acts as a sliding window, so every new bit checks a new candidate. No external hardware is required beyond the clock, reset, and two input pins.

This circuit implements a sequential rear-light controller inspired by the Ford Thunderbird, using a 2-bit counter and decoders to produce progressive left and right light patterns. The blinker input selects left, right, both, or neither sequence, and the outputs drive three LEDs per side. The design is tested by applying reset, setting blinker values, and observing the output progression over several clock cycles. It was created as part of the IEEE OpenSilicon Bootcamp and requires external LEDs for visual output.

This design is an interactive tile growth simulator for a 16x16 WS2812B LED matrix, where players place colored cells and then start a random growth process. It uses a 16-bit LFSR seeded by player cursor movements to drive the spreading of colors into empty neighbors until the grid is full. The design is tested with a cocotb testbench that runs three starting configurations and prints the grid state after each round. External hardware includes the 16x16 LED matrix and pushbuttons for input.
